name: Mushtaq
definition: Mushtaq is a composite portrait of a Muslim wholesale fruit trader in Hosapete town, Ballari district, whose fortunes depend on the grape harvest from the irrigated Tungabhadra command and whose business connects him daily to the APMC market, lorry transporters and the stream of visitors to nearby Hampi. He represents the trading communities that anchor Hosapete's bazaar economy and the multilingual, multi-faith character of this town at the edge of Kalyana Karnataka and the ruins of the Vijayanagara Empire.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Mushtaq runs a wholesale fruit stall at Hosapete's APMC market, specialising in grapes brought in from farms along the Tungabhadra Left Bank Canal around Sindhanur and Manvi. His day begins at four in the morning when the trucks arrive; he grades the fruit, negotiates with commission agents and arranges onward transport to Bengaluru and Hyderabad. The income is good during the January-March grape season, bringing in perhaps thirty to forty thousand rupees a month when harvests are strong, but it swings sharply with yield and price. The rest of the year he trades pomegranates, bananas and whatever else moves, and earnings drop to half or less. He employs two assistants, usually young men from his mohalla, and owns a small Tata Ace for local pickups. The pressure is constant: perishable stock, tight credit from wholesalers in Bengaluru, and the diesel and labour costs that eat into margins. Hosapete's economy hums with the steel plant at nearby Toranagallu and Hampi tourism, so there is cash flow, but the fruit trade remains volatile and dependent on the canal water reaching the farms on time.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Mushtaq lives with his wife Fareeda, their three children and his widowed mother in a three-room house in a Muslim-majority lane near the Jama Masjid in Hosapete town. His wife manages the household, cooks, cares for his mother and helps their eldest daughter, now sixteen, prepare for her second-year PUC exams. Their second child, a son aged thirteen, is in eighth standard, and the youngest daughter is nine and in fourth standard. Fareeda wanted to take up tailoring work at home, but Mushtaq prefers she focus on the children's schooling, a decision they still debate. His mother, now in her seventies, is diabetic and needs regular medication. Gender roles in the household follow traditional lines: Fareeda does not work outside, Mushtaq controls the income and major decisions, and the girls are expected to help with cooking and cleaning after school. The family speaks Dakhni Urdu at home, Kannada in the market and a bit of Telugu with suppliers from across the border. Marriage is on the horizon for their eldest daughter, and Mushtaq is setting aside what he can for her wedding and dowry, a worry that keeps him awake at night.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Mushtaq studied up to seventh standard in an Urdu-medium school in Hosapete before leaving to help his father in the same fruit business. He regrets not finishing school and is determined his children will do better. His eldest daughter attends the government junior college in Hosapete for her PUC in the commerce stream; she travels there by auto, which costs about two hundred rupees a week. His son is in a Kannada-medium municipal school nearby, within walking distance, and the youngest daughter is in the same school. School fees are minimal, but the PUC coaching classes, textbooks and auto fare add up to several thousand rupees a term. Mushtaq wants his son to aim for a government job, perhaps in the railways or a clerk position, something with a steady salary and pension. For his daughters, he wants them to finish PUC and perhaps a BA, though he expects both will marry soon after; the eldest has already received a proposal from a family in Raichur. The children study in Kannada medium because that is what the better local schools offer, and Mushtaq believes it will give them more opportunities than Urdu medium, though his mother sometimes laments they cannot read the Quran as fluently as she did.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Health access in Hosapete is better than in the surrounding villages, with a government hospital, a few private clinics and a couple of decent pharmacies in the bazaar. Mushtaq's mother sees a private doctor for her diabetes, costing about five hundred rupees a visit plus another thousand a month for medicines; government doctors are free but the wait is long and she prefers the private clinic. His wife had a difficult delivery with their youngest daughter and needed a caesarean at a private nursing home, which put them fifteen thousand rupees in debt that took two years to clear. The children fall ill with fever and cough during the monsoon, treated at home with over-the-counter medicines and the occasional doctor visit. Mushtaq himself has chronic acidity, which he blames on irregular meals and the stress of the market, and he takes antacids daily. He has heard of the Ayushman Bharat scheme but has never applied for a card, unsure of the paperwork and assuming it would not cover his mother's ongoing diabetes treatment. Drinking water comes from a borewell in the lane, and everyone knows the water in parts of Hosapete and the canal belt can have fluoride, though Mushtaq has never had his family tested. The fear of serious illness, an accident or a major hospital bill is ever-present, and he has no health insurance.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Mushtaq's family belongs to the Dakhni-speaking Muslim community that has lived in Hosapete for generations, historically linked to trade and small business rather than farming. The mohalla where he lives is tight-knit, and Friday prayers at the Jama Masjid anchor the week. His mother is devout and insists the children learn Quranic recitation at the local madrasa, though Mushtaq is more relaxed, attending prayers on Fridays and Eid but not every day. Ties to the Khwaja Bande Nawaz Dargah in Kalaburagi are strong; the family makes the trip for the annual urs when they can afford it, and his mother has a framed picture of the dargah on the wall. Relations with Hindu neighbours and business partners are mostly cordial; the APMC market is mixed, and trust and credit flow across community lines in everyday trade. But Mushtaq is conscious of the political climate, the talk around the country about Muslims, and the occasional tension around Eid processions or Ganesh festival routes. He avoids political arguments, keeps his head down and focuses on business. Within the community, the mosque committee and local ulema wield influence, especially on questions of marriage, inheritance and religious schooling, and Mushtaq respects their authority even when he quietly disagrees.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Mushtaq's main dealings with government are through the APMC market, where he pays fees and relies on the market yard's infrastructure and the commission agents who mediate between farmers and traders. He has never attended a gram sabha or town municipal meeting and would not know how to raise an issue there. He applied once for a bank loan to expand his stall, but the paperwork and collateral demands defeated him, and he borrowed from a private moneylender instead. His family has ration cards, and they collect subsidised rice and kerosene from the fair-price shop, though the shop is often out of stock or closed at odd hours. He has heard of Gruha Jyothi and Gruha Lakshmi but does not fully understand how they work; his wife uses the Shakti free bus scheme occasionally to visit her parents in Raichur, which has saved them money. Mushtaq has little faith that government schemes reach people like him; he sees the schemes announced, the banners put up, but in practice it is the well-connected or those with influence who benefit. He blames neither the local officer nor the system in the abstract, but simply accepts that this is how things work.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Mushtaq worries most about price volatility in the grape market, the cost of his daughter's wedding, his mother's health and whether his son will find stable work in a government job or fall into the same precarious trading life. He is proud of Hosapete's location next to Hampi, the tourists who pass through and the steel-plant jobs that keep money circulating in the town, but he also sees the gap between the heritage tourism promoted by the government and the lack of investment in schools, hospitals and roads in the neighbourhoods where ordinary people like him live. He resents the stereotype, sometimes voiced by people from Bengaluru or coastal Karnataka, that this region is backward or not really Kannada; he speaks Kannada every day in the market, his children study in Kannada, and he is as much a Kannadiga as anyone, even if Urdu is his home language. He blames the long neglect under the Nizam and then by Karnataka governments for the region's difficulties, and he sees Article 371(J) as a recognition of that neglect, though he is not sure what it has delivered on the ground. He wants his children to have the education and security he never had, and he is willing to work brutal hours in the market to give them that chance. But he also knows that without connections, without someone in government or a steady salaried job, families like his remain one bad season or one medical emergency away from serious trouble. What he demands is simple: fair prices, reliable canal water for the farmers he depends on, decent schools and hospitals that work, and a government that treats Muslims as equal citizens rather than a political problem to be managed or mobilised at election time.
